did_you_know.text: The chapter describes Leviathan using two images: “the fleeing serpent” and “the twisting serpent”; it also calls him “the dragon that is in the sea.”
Israel is compared to “a vineyard of wine,” and the verse calls for a song about it; the vineyard image is used in the chapter to describe the people of Israel.
The LORD is described as the keeper of the vineyard: He waters it “continually” and watches over it without pause, “night and day.”
Instead of lasting anger, the LORD offers the possibility of peace; if thorns and briers stand against Him in battle, He will burn them all together.
The verse invites an enemy or opponent to take hold of the LORD’s stronghold and make peace with Him—and it repeats the word “peace” twice.
The chapter describes a future of flourishing for Jacob and Israel: they will take root, bud, and blossom, and their produce will fill the whole world.

The prophet presents Israel’s punishment as not necessarily equivalent to the punishment of its enemies, raising the question of how Israel’s punishment differs from that of the nations that attacked it.
The punishment is described as measured—“by measure”—and in connection with a harsh wind and a day of east wind; this wording emphasizes both the measured nature and the severity of the blow.
Jacob’s guilt will be atoned for through the removal of sin and the destruction of idolatry: the stones of the altars will be shattered, and the Asherah poles and incense altars will rise no more.

On that day the LORD will gather the Israelites one by one from the region between the Euphrates River and the Wadi of Egypt; in the next verse, the blowing of a great trumpet will gather the lost and scattered to worship in Jerusalem.
